In screw theory, a screw (FR: torseur) is a pair of related three dimensional vectors. It is used as an analytic tool in rigid body motions.<ref>{{#cite:Q1848}}</ref>

== History ==

In the 1830s, French mathematician [[Person:Michel Chasles|Michel Chasles]] demonstrated that any rigid body displacement can be decomposed into a rotation about a unique axis combined with a translation. This idea laid the foundation for Irish astronomer [[Person:Robert Ball|Robert Ball]] to systematise the idea into structured algebra in his 1900 treatise ''A Treatise on the Theory of Screws''. His work has since be modernised to form the modern screw theory based on dual-vectors.<ref>{{#cite:Q1860}}</ref>

== Mathematical definition ==

Let $\vec{R}$, $\vec M$ be vectors of $\mathbb R^3$

=== Classic screw ===

If for arbitrary points in space $A,B$:

$$
\vec R_B=\vec R_A \\
\vec{M_B}=\vec M_A+ \overrightarrow{BA}\wedge \vec{R}
$$

Then $\mathcal{\{T\}}=\left\{\begin{matrix}\vec R \\ \vec M\end{matrix}\right\}$ is a '''screw''' in this space. $\vec{R}$ is called the '''resultant, and $\vec M_A$ the '''moment''' at $A$.<ref>{{#cite:Q1851}}</ref>

<blockquote>
Notice:

* The resultant is spatially-independent,
** i.e., it is the same at every point in space;
* The moment is spatially-dependent,
** i.e., a change in reference point results in a change in moment.
</blockquote>

=== Integrated screw ===

Let $dp$ be an element of system $K$ at $P$, then for arbitrary point in space $A$

$$
\{\mathcal{U}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\displaystyle \int_K \vec{R}(P)\,dp \\[6pt]
\displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP
\end{Bmatrix}_A .
$$

is an '''integrated screw'''.

It satisfies the property:

$$
\displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{BP}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP= \displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP + \displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{BA}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP
$$

analog to classic screws.

== Screws describing forces and torques ==

A wrench describes external forces on a solid or a system and their associated moments, also known as '''torques''', according to a reference point.

=== Wrench (discrete forces) ===

If a solid or system experiences $n$ external forces $\vec F_i$ each exerted on point $M_i$, its wrench '''according to reference point $A$''' is:

$$
\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{n}}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\sum_{i=1}^n \vec{F}_{i} \\
\sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{AM_i}\times \vec{F}_{i}
\end{Bmatrix}_A
$$

== Screw describing the motion of solid $S$ ==

=== Twist ===

Wrench is the screw of the rotational velocity vector of solid $S$ according to a given reference and its associated moment vector, the linear velocity vector at a given point.

$$
\mathcal{\{V}(S/R)\}_A=\left\{\begin{matrix}\vec \omega_{S/R} \\ \vec v_{A,S/R}\end{matrix}\right\}
$$

==== Composition for complex movements ====

As motion is relative, according to a different reference system, the velocity of the solid will be different.

In general, for a point $A$ on solid $(S)$ in motion according to reference system $R_1$, its motion according to another reference system $R_0$ is:

$$
$\begin{cases}
\vec \omega_{S/R_0}=\vec \omega_{S/R_1}+\vec \omega_{R_1/R_0} \\
\vec v_{A,S/R_0}=\vec v_{A,S/R_1}+\vec v_{A \in R_1/R_0}
\end{cases}
$

Where

$$
\vec v_{A \in R_1/R_0}=\vec v_{O_1,R_1/R_0}+\overrightarrow{MO_1}\wedge \vec \omega_{R_1/R_0}
$$

is the velocity of $A$ in $R_0$ of $A$ is static according to $R_1$.

Furthermore, the acceleration vector can be derived by differentiation:

$$
\vec a_{A,S/R_0}=(\frac{d\vec v_{A,S/R_0}}{dt})_{R_0}
$$

Which gives

$$
\vec a_{A,S/R_0}=\vec a_{A,S/R_1}+\vec a_{A \in R_1/R_0}+2\vec \omega_{R_1/R_0} \wedge \vec v_{A,S/R_1}
$$

<blockquote>
Notice that the acceleration of point $A$ according to $R_0$ is more than the sum of its acceleration according to $R_1$ and the acceleration of $R_1$ according to $R_0$ at point $A$. The additional term, $2\vec \omega_{R_1/R_0} \wedge \vec v_{A,S/R_1}$, is known as '''Coriolis complementary acceleration'''.
</blockquote>

where

$$
\vec a_{A \in R_1/R_0}=\vec a_{O_1,R_1/R_0}+(x_{A/R_1}\frac{d^2\vec i_1}{dt^2})_{R_0}+(y_{A/R_1}\frac{d^2\vec j_1}{dt^2})_{R_0}+(z_{A/R_1}\frac{d^2\vec k_1}{dt^2})_{R_0}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q1854}}</ref>

== Screws describing the motion of system $K$ ==

=== Kinetic screw ===

kinetic screw represents the momentum of a system $K$ and its moment according to a given reference point.

$$
\{\mathcal{K}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\int_S \vec{v}(M)\,dm=m\vec{v}(C) \\
\int_S \overrightarrow{AM}\times \vec{v}(M)\,dm
\end{Bmatrix}_A
$$

where $C$ is always the centre of mass and $\vec{v}(M)$ is the velocity of the mass element $dm$ in the chosen reference frame.

=== Dynamic screw ===

The dynamic screw represents the acceleration of a system $K$ and its moment according to a given reference point.

$$
\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\int_K \vec{a}(M)\,dm=m\vec{a}(C) \\
\int_K \overrightarrow{AM}\times \vec{a}(M)\,dm
\end{Bmatrix}_A
$$

where $C$ is always the centre of mass and $\vec{a}(M)$ is the acceleration of the mass element $dm$ in the chosen reference frame.

== Fundamental principle of dynamics ==

The '''fundamental principle of dynamics''' of screw theory states

$$
\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}\}_A
$$

where $\{\mathcal{D}\}$ is [[#Dynamic_screw|the dynamic screw]] and $\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}\}_A$ is [[#Wrench_(discrete_forces)|the wrench]]
